subQuestions.questionText: Indicate whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE: A credit balance on the Bank Statement means that the business has a positive balance in the bank.
subQuestions.memoText:
True (1 mark)
From the bank's perspective, a credit balance on the bank statement represents money owed to the business — i.e. a favourable/positive balance for the business.
Accept T/F.

subQuestions.questionText: Indicate whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE: A debit card may be used to withdraw cash from an ATM.
subQuestions.memoText:
True (1 mark)
A debit card draws funds directly from the cardholder's bank account and can be used at an ATM to withdraw cash.
Accept T/F.

subQuestions.questionText: Indicate whether the following statement is TRUE or FALSE: A bank overdraft is a short-term loan that is transferred into the business current bank account.
subQuestions.memoText:
False (1 mark)
A bank overdraft is a facility that allows the account to go into a negative balance up to a pre-arranged limit; it is not transferred as a separate loan into the current account.
Accept T/F.

subQuestions.questionText: Violet noticed problems with the depositing of cash. Explain TWO measures that she can use to address these problems.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid points (2 marks each = 4 marks). Part marks for incomplete/unclear responses. Must relate to cash deposits of the business.

Acceptable answers include:
• Implement a depositing routine/policy on daily or regular depositing.
• Employ a different person to be responsible for depositing money (division of duties — 1 mark only).
• Engage the services of a cash-in-transit (security) company / split large amounts into smaller deposits.
• Supervise / conduct independent check / authorise funds before depositing / inspect deposit slips before and after.
• Encourage more customers to pay by EFT (less cash handling).
• Set up bank notification (SMS) service for all transactions.
• Do regular or random reconciliations using mini-statements from the banking app as an interim control; reconcile cash and card transactions daily to avoid later errors.

subQuestions.questionText: Comment on the stockholding periods of the Pacific and Caspian TV sets. Explain how the different holding periods affect the business financially. Explain what these periods indicate about the preferences of the customers. Quote figures or calculations.
subQuestions.memoText:
Three sub-parts (4 + 4 + 4 = 12 marks).

PART A — Comment on stockholding periods (4 marks):
Comment on Pacific ✓ + figure ✓:
  SHP of 184 days (≈6 months) is long; older model that may not sell in future. A decrease in units sold resulted in a high stock value of R3 580 500 (see 2.2.1) and lower profits.
Comment on Caspian ✓ + figure ✓:
  SHP of 71 days (≈2,3 months) is acceptable — new, durable, in demand.
*Accept combined answer: e.g. 113 days or 3,8 months (two marks).

PART B — Financial impact (4 marks):
Explanation for Pacific ✓ + figure(s) ✓:
  Pacific places strain on cash flow. High closing stock (R3 580 500) and slower rate of sales (from 250 → 110 units) means money is tied up in stock / requires more liquid assets / additional expenses (insurance, storage, possible obsolescence/damage).
Explanation for Caspian ✓ + figure(s) ✓:
  Caspian sells well; 340 & 330 in two quarters / sales revenue R5 548 800 + R5 385 600 = R10 934 400; better gross profit (R4 100 400 — see 2.2.2) / minimises pressure on liquidity / will recoup investment soon.

PART C — Customer preferences (4 marks):
Explanation ✓✓ (mention both brands or implied):
  Customers not interested in the Pacific (old technology) / negatively affected by introduction of newer brand. They prefer the newer, more expensive Caspian.
Figures ✓✓ (comparison of each brand):
  Gradual lowering of SP from R13 500 → R9 800 (Pacific) did not influence customers.
  They are prepared to pay more for Caspian: R16 320 vs R9 800 — better quality/features.
  Compare 110 vs 330 / 160 vs 340 / 270 vs 670 units.
  Caspian sells faster: 83,75% of available units sold vs 66,5% of Pacific.

• Extend target market (other areas, guesthouses, hotels).

subQuestions.questionText:
Direct material and direct labour: Refer to Information A and C. Lez made specific decisions to improve the business and its product. Explain how the decisions he took have benefited the business by providing:
• TWO separate points relating to the raw material (with figures or calculations)
• TWO separate points relating to the direct labour (with figures or calculations)
subQuestions.memoText:
Two parts (6 + 6 = 12 marks).

RAW MATERIAL — Any TWO different points explained ✓✓✓✓ + specific figure(s) for each ✓✓ (6 marks):
• Prepared to pay a higher price for better quality material — Paid R200 (R110 in 2022) / R90 or 81,8% more per metre.
• Higher price did not deter customers — 4 000 more shirts sold / SP increased from R1 430 → R1 830 / by R400 / by 28%.
• Good quality material resulted in less wastage — Used 1,8 m per shirt (vs 2,5 m in 2022). Used 43 200 m for 10 500 shirts (vs 44 000 m for 6 500 shirts) / 800 m or 1,8% less.

DIRECT LABOUR — Any TWO different points explained ✓✓✓✓ + specific figure(s) for each ✓✓ (6 marks):
• Better recruitment and training → more motivated/efficient workforce. Produced 4 000 extra units / 62% more in 2023. Average output per worker increased from 433 → 875 shirts / 442 more / 5,5 shirts/hour vs 3,4 shirts/hour.
• Investment in equipment and training → reduced direct labour cost. DLC decreased by R24 000 / DLC per unit decreased from R148 → R89 / by 40%.
• Decreased number of workers, paid higher average wage (skill recognition) → better performance. From 15 → 12 workers / Average wage from R64 000 → R78 000 / by R14 000 / 22%.
• Maintained hours per worker but total hours dropped → drop in total wages without harming production. 1 920 hours per worker / total hours dropped from 28 800 → 23 040 / by 5 760 / 20%. DLC decreased by R24 000.

Be alert to the same point expressed differently. Part marks for incomplete/unclear responses.

• Provide TWO suggestions on how Alice can improve the use or efficiency of the vehicles.
subQuestions.memoText:
Four sub-parts (4 + 2 + 4 + 4 = 14 marks).

PART A — Advertising effectiveness (4 marks). Figures from Information F (May) must be quoted.
Comment ✓✓ + comparative figures ✓✓ (must compare percentages; one mark only if amounts only):
• Sales is lower than budget by 15% (191 100 / 1 274 000) but advertising is lower by only 3,7% (1 400 / 38 220).
• Advertising is budgeted at 3% of sales (38 220 / 1 274 000); actual is 3,4% of sales (36 820 / 1 082 900).
Part marks for partial response (advertising or sales only).

PART B — Justify control over delivery expenses (2 marks; one part correct). Calculation must involve the 5% target:
Workings: 1 082 900 × 5% = R54 145
  OR 54 145 – 54 100 = R45 difference
  OR 63 700 – 54 100 = R9 600 (one mark option)
Answer: 4,9% or 5% ✓✓ (one part correct)
  OR R54 145 ✓✓
  OR R45 ✓✓
*Note: 54 100 ÷ 1 082 900 × 100 alone is not 'one part correct'.

PART C — Issue for EACH vehicle (4 marks: 2 per vehicle):
Vehicle 1 — Problem ✓ + figure ✓ (any ONE):
• High maintenance: R9 500 of R16 000 / 59% of budget.
• Used 65,6% of total delivery expenses (R35 500 of R54 100).
• High kilometres covered: 1 260 km of 1 800 km / 70% of workload.
• Vehicle 1 is 4 years older than V2 and is being over-used (1 260 km).

Vehicle 2 — Problem ✓ + figure ✓ (any ONE):
• Under-utilised: only 540 km / 30% of workload / 720 km less than V1.
• Used R14 000 of R40 000 for fuel / 35% of fuel budget — possible abuse.
• Delivery expenses average R34,44 per km vs R28,17 (V1) or R31,85 (budget).
• Paid same R15 000 salary while being unproductive.

PART D — TWO suggestions to improve vehicle use/efficiency (4 marks; 2 marks each). Part marks for incomplete/unclear responses:
• Keep a logbook of trips covered and supervise regularly.
• Set targets for each driver per week/month / balance workload per vehicle.
• Plan regular maintenance/servicing for long-term productivity.
• Pay drivers per work covered instead of fixed salary (incentive/motivation).
• Install GPS tracking to minimise abuse / prevent personal use.
• Swap use of vehicles — older for shorter trips, newer for longer trips.
• Combine loads/consignments going in the same direction / determine tariffs based on distance.
